newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbs dress up for protest, but numbers thinner.
newsitem.headline: Serbs dress up for protest, but numbers thinner.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Serbians dressed in fatigues, postal uniforms and hospital garb rallied in Belgrade on Saturday for another demonstration to demand restoration of annulled local election results.

In a carnival-like atmosphere, some 30,000 protesters heeded the call of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition to wear uniforms as they demonstrated in front of hundreds of uniformed riot police in the city centre.
Some wore gas masks, one person brought a white poodle dressed in a camouflage outfit and another was spotted carrying a Confederate flag from the American Civil War.
"This is a spontaneous civil revolt against the regime," said Misa, 42, a retired federal policeman, who wore an old combat uniform of the special forces.

Other people were dressed as housewives, workers with hard hats or students and one older woman wore the kit of a hockey player. One man appeared as a chef, sporting a tall, white hat and brandishing a huge ladle.
Banners proclaimed: "I'll be here tomorrow, too", "Bill (Clinton), drink in the spirit of Belgrade" and "Serbia is in its third month" (of pregnancy).
Earlier, students ended an all-night confrontation with police who withdrew early in the morning and allowed about 3,000 demonstrators to march around the city centre.
Opposition leaders had called for a massive demonstration in the afternoon to show that protests to force the government to reinstate the election results were still going strong.

But the crowd was little bigger than it has been for the last few days, with numbers well down on the 100,000 a day who rallied over the past two months of protests against autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist government.
"I am hopeful but I do not have any illusions. The authorities do not want to change anything by peaceful means," said Zoran, a 35-year-old bank clerk in the crowd.
"This is a war of nerves. The problem is there is no general rebellion, no workers.
"Although they are out of work, only one in 10 comes to the protest," he said, referring to lack of blue collar support.

The protesters are demanding the restoration of Zajedno victories in municipal elections last November in 14 big Serbian cities, including the capital Belgrade, which were annulled by the government due to alleged "irregularities".
International pressure has been building on the government to reinstate the election results but so far the Socialists have made few concessions.

Political sources said Socialist hardliners planned to lodge an appeal against an election commission ruling restoring the Zajedno victory in Belgrade, but as of late Saturday there was no word that an appeal had been filed.

Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno leader, told the afternoon rally: "For 60 days the whole world has been watching us and everyone has been waiting for something to happen, for the authorities to do something.
"But what is the only man who needs to do something doing? -- reconstructing his government," Djindjic said, referring to an announcement by Milosevic that he plans to reshuffle his cabinet.
"When we get the new government, there will be even more empty pots and pans in Serbia for people to bang at 7.30 every evening," Djindjic added.
Thousands of people bang pots and pans and blow whistles every night to drown out the news broadcast on Serbian television, which pays scant attention to the protest campaign.
